newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Bangemann says French-German postal deal no compromise.
newsitem.headline: Bangemann says French-German postal deal no compromise.

text.p: Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann has made it clear he is not happy with a deal between France and Germany that would delay liberalisation of European Union postal services.

"The French-German compromise is very close to the position of those who don't want very much liberalisation. It is not really a compromise," Bangemann told the European Parliament's transport committee earlier this week.
France and Germany have agreed to back a text that would put off until at least 2003 a plan to open competition in the direct mail and cross-border mail sectors.
Bangemann said most member states, including the Netherlands, which takes over the EU presidency on January 1, 1997, did not see the French-German deal as a compromise.
The Telecommunications Council is set to discuss draft directive COM(95)227 on postal services at its meeting next week.
EU member states are divided over how quickly to allow private operators to compete with state post offices to deliver direct mail and cross-border mail.
The Irish presidency has proposed that direct mail be liberalised by January 1, 2001 and that ministers pledge to adopt measures by that date on further liberalisation of the sector.
But France, Belgium, Greece, Portugal and Luxembourg have resisted setting a date for opening up direct mail.
Germany and France have now agreed a plan under which the EU would decide by 2001 whether to open up direct and cross-border mail, but that no steps would actually be taken before 2003.
Bangemann insisted that only a genuine compromise could break the deadlock in the Council, where Britain, Sweden, Finland and the Netherlands were demanding speedy liberalisation.
He insisted that deregulation was unavoidable, both to create a proper internal market in postal services and because the sector would collapse if it did not move with the times.
"I don't think a public monopoly in this area can survive (given the pace of) technological development," he said.
Postponing deregulation would only hasten the demise of the post office because dissatisfied customers would turn to other services, such as fax and electronic mail, he stressed.

He warned that unless member states agreed a directive soon, the Commission would have to take the unsatisfactory step of taking member states to the European Court of Justice under Article 90 of the EC treaty to force them to respect EU competition law, he warned.

Bangemann said the Commission was not proposing a hard and fast date for liberalisation but believed that setting some kind of timeframe was unavoidable, even if this was subsequently altered in the light of experience.
"We are in favour of a timeline but with a revision clause," he said, adding that a majority of member states appeared to favour a 2001 deadline.
He noted that the Commission had promised to publish a communication on the application of EU competition rules to postal services by the end of 1996.
He assured MEPs this would not be used to create a new legal base for EU laws on postal services but would set out guidelines saying how the Commission should apply Article 90 to the sector.
